questions.q: What are the three standard stages of the signal construction pipeline described in this lesson?
options: Backtest, optimize, execute
Transform, normalize, lag
Collect, clean, delete
Buy, hold, sell
questions.explain: Almost every signal goes through transform (compute the raw quantity), normalize (put it on a comparable scale), and lag (shift it forward to avoid using future information).

questions.q: What is the difference between cross-sectional and time-series normalization?
options: They produce identical results, just computed differently
Cross-sectional compares instruments to each other at one point in time; time-series compares a value to its own history
Cross-sectional only works for currencies
Time-series normalization cannot use rolling windows
questions.explain: A cross-sectional rank or z-score compares peers at the same date ("is this cheaper than others right now"), while a time-series z-score compares a value to its own historical distribution ("is this high relative to how it usually behaves").

questions.q: Why does winsorizing a signal matter, especially after z-scoring?
options: It increases the total number of data points
It caps extreme outliers so a single bad data point or extreme event doesn't single-handedly dominate a combined signal or sizing decision
It removes the need for normalization entirely
It guarantees the signal will be profitable
questions.explain: Z-scores are unbounded, so one extreme outlier can swamp everything else once signals are combined or used for sizing. Winsorizing caps the value at a threshold while preserving its relative ordering information.

questions.q: A signal is computed using today's closing price, and the backtest then assumes this signal could be used to trade at today's close. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong — the signal and the trade use the same date
This leaks future information into the trading decision; the signal must be shifted forward at least one bar before being used to trade
The signal should instead use tomorrow's close
Closing prices cannot be used in any signal
questions.explain: Using today's close to inform a trade executed at today's close assumes knowledge you wouldn't actually have at that moment. Shifting the signal forward by at least one bar is the mechanical fix for this lookahead bug.

questions.q: Before sending a signal to a backtest, which of these is a reasonable sanity check according to this lesson?
options: Confirming the signal is constant across all time periods
Confirming the signal visibly varies over time and doesn't have a single outlier swamping the rest of its distribution
Confirming the signal always predicts positive returns
Confirming the signal uses no historical data at all
questions.explain: A signal that's frozen or constant for long stretches usually indicates a rolling-window bug, and an unchecked outlier distribution usually indicates a missing winsorization step — both worth catching before backtesting.
